utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, case number IT-04-74-PT, the Prosecutor against Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, Slobodan Praljak, Milivoj Petkovic, Valentin Coric, and Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. First, for the record, I'd like to explain that we're here only with one accused present and his counsel. That's Mr. Prlic. Counsel, Mr. Par, who is mainly here to answer a few questions since he's also participating in the Defence of Mr. Martinovic. This hearing is a continued hearing from yesterday where the Chamber seeks additional information in order to determine whether representation by counsel of three accused in this case can be accepted or not. I see that for the Prosecution, Mr. Scott, you are present at this moment. You were not present yesterday. I take it that you understand the limited role of the Prosecution in this hearing. Mainly, I would say, not in any way to interfere with choice of counsel by an accused but only to make observations which could be useful to determine whether it could lead to any disruption of the trial at later stages, which would certainly have its effect on the Office of the Prosecutor as well. That's understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Kenneth Scott for the record. Your Honour, we do understand the role that you've indicated. We appreciate the opportunity to be here. Of course, when we learned that it was a public hearing, I guess my initial instinct was if it was a public hearing that there's a -- that the Prosecutor should, out of honour and responsibility as much as anything else, should be present and play whatever role or not that the Chamber would ask us to play. So we understand and we appreciate the Chamber having us here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Par, we did not finish yet yesterday on a few issues. What would be your position if Mr. Martinovic in a later stage would be called as a witness either by the Chamber or by the Prosecution, or would you consider it even possible to call Mr. Martinovic as a witness for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not consider the possibility of calling him as a Defence witness since I believe that these two case are not connected in any way. How I would -- what my position towards Martinovic would depend on the specific circumstances. As his Defence counsel, I would know all the circumstances of that testimony, so I would consider that as if he -- as if the Prlic case were some third case. So I cannot really answer this hypothetical question, but I know that I would take my position in accordance with the consequences and the circumstances which would lead possibly to such testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you think that if Mr. Martinovic would be called either by the Prosecution or by the Trial Chamber that you could ask him questions based upon your knowledge that you gained during your defence of Mr. Martinovic if they would be in favour of Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't see myself in the courtroom in such a situation. I don't see myself in the courtroom in such a situation at all. Far from it that I should ask him questions or -- I cannot be with Martinovic in the position of being his Defence counsel and to ask him questions from the point of view of another case. This is something that cannot happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if he's called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Martinovic is called to testify, if Martinovic decides to testify, then I would find a way out of that situation by leaving it in the hands of the lead counsel, because I am, after all, a co-counsel in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think you couldn't examine him as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would never wish to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Whether you wish to do it is not the question. The question is whether you're allowed to do it according to your own standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear. And let me ask you the following question: In respect of the position of Mr. Prlic as a civilian, do you consider it possible that a civilian authority exercises any power or any control over military men?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Theoretically, yes, but in the specific case I believe that that would not be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say you do not believe that although this is theoretically possible that it happened in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you consider -- in view of this question, do you consider Mr. Martinovic a real military man who would not be subject to a civilian authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm glad that Mr. Scott is also here. From the beginning to the end of the Martinovic defence, his position regarding his position and the position of his superiors was always the same. It did not change from the beginning to the end, and that position was that he was the commander of the lowest-ranking military formation and that the commander of the town of Mostar was the commander for the units which were on the line of separation. That was the end and the beginning of Martinovic's connection with the superiors, and that is what -- what has stayed unchanged from the beginning to the end in the Martinovic Defence. This can be also expressed by the Prosecution. Throughout his defence, he denied any connections with any form of civilian power, with politicians. He continually stressed in his defence - this is what his defence was based on - that he did not have anything to do with any structures of authority in any possible way. He was not receiving instructions from them, and he did not participate in any other circumstances together with them. So based on that defence, he said, "I entered that war defending my home as a regular soldier, defending it first of all in the war against the Croats, then in the war against the Muslims," and he ruled out decisively any connection with any kind of military or civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could one say that Mr. Martinovic would be involved in a quasi-military, quasi-civil defence structure?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout these proceedings he was not treated in that way by the Prosecution either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you as Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a Defence counsel, I was on that case from the stand position -- from the position that he was a member of a self-organised unit which later joined the organisation under the command of the city of Mostar which shaped them in that particular way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Command -- civil command or military command?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was under the military command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I read to you from the final brief in the Martinovic case: "The accused is not a military commander in the sense envisaged in terms of traditional motions of command responsibility. He was a civilian who through the circumstances pertaining in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the early 1990s voluntarily participated in a form of Civil Defence." And in paragraph 84, the Defence has argued that the extent to which the command responsibility theory could be applied is narrower in the case of an informal quasi-military, quasi-civil defence structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I stated before, the position of the Defence is that Vinko Martinovic first joined the conflict against the Serbs in a way that the group of people he was with self-organised in the fight against the Serbs. At the beginning of the conflict against the Muslims, the Bosniaks, that same group of people which up to that time was self-organised, after they set up the line of separation became a unit. So from a voluntarily based civilian status, it crossed over by the nature of things into a military status because there was a need for those people, the civilians who were defending a part of the town, to be organised in some shape or form. So therefore, he was forced by circumstances to become a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not as a member of any paramilitary structure, but it was just a unit which was formed in accordance with the nature of that war, that conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you another question? You have mentioned in one of the submissions that one Judge may sit on both cases, Martinovic and Mr. Prlic. Could you please explain to me how the composition of a Trial Chamber could impact on the existence or the non-existence of a conflict of interest?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said, Your Honour, that His Honour Judge Liu was following my work, the defence in that case, and I also said that my learned friend Mr. Scott also followed the development of that case, and I thought that in that way there was some kind of control over my work. This is what I thought, that I simply could not, even if I wanted to, exceed the boundaries that have been established here. I thought that that was a well-known argument that will go to my favour, that there was absolutely some way to monitor my work. That's all I thought. In any case, the Prosecution is in the position to know all the information that is available to me from one case and to the information that they have provided me from a different case. They're in a position to know that better than the Trial Chamber which has not received that material so far. So the Prosecution can always react if they saw that I was in any way abusing my position by using information that I'm not supposed to use. This is something that I thought would work in my favour in that away that there's an overview and a clear picture of my position, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the Prosecution is concerned, they have expressed an opinion which is not very much in favour of you to continue working in the case of Mr. Prlic. I mean, if you say that's something that would be of guidance to me, then I'm a bit surprised to hear this, because the Prosecution was firmly opposing against your representation of Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to resolve this question immediately by asking, if it's possible, Mr. Scott. The Prosecution was against my appointment. I understood that. This was because of a theoretical or a hypothetical grounds, because a possible conflict of interest in my case is being brought to a sort of theoretical or abstract level, and I'm struggling with it before you today and yesterday, because these are all hypothetical questions, and I do not see any true answer that I could give to you. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond However, along with that we have a real situation. These two cases, these two defendants and myself, and these people here who took part in these cases are all here. I thought that we were all reasonable people, that -- I simply thought that we had a real feeling for this realistic or actual situation here. If we're talking about the position of the Prosecution towards me, then in that case I would like to hear that from them here today. I would like to have an answer to this. In any case, Your Honour, I believe that the real situation, as we have before us, does not place me into any conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you say there is no conflict of interest at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot see it either in -- at this moment or in future moments. I would like to have my other client here and then you would be able to see both clients hearing what you asked me, what I answered, and then they could say, "We think it is or isn't." So I don't think this is a conflict of interest now, nor that I will be in future, and I went into this point at several levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is the position your present clients take most important for you for your assessment on whether there would be a risk of a conflict of interest?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I decide whether there is a conflict of interest, I myself looked into my own conscience and decided this, looking at the two cases, and the decisive factor for me was whether I see the possibility of finding myself in a position of conflict of interest. That's a position I do not wish to find myself in. Once I've done that, the next thing that's important for me is, from the point of view of both clients, to look at all the aspects that we're discussing here today, and the important thing for me is whether they place their trust in me and give me the go-ahead. And it is, of course, my obligation to be loyal to the confidence and trust they place in me. But I don't doubt that either -- that my clients trust me fully and have confidence in me. I don't think they are afraid that I will inflict any damage. But of course it would be best for you to ask them, to ask then whether they fear that there could be a conflict of interest in view of their defence case and the kind of person I am. You could ask them whether they are afraid of having any detrimental effects, this having any detrimental effects on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You invited me to ask Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, did I understand the position of the Prosecution well that they strongly oppose of representation of Mr. Prlic by Mr. Par because of the risk of a conflict of interest to arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In a word, Your Honour, yes, that's the Prosecution's position. I've taken with great reluctance. It has nothing to do with Mr. Par personally but the situation as it exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think I've got no further questions for you, Mr. Par. Therefore, I'd like to ask -- I don't know whether you've scheduled any order among counsel, which one to be next asked questions about this issue. Mr. Olujic, if I have the accent right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Salahovic and Mr. Par, you are free to stay. This is a public hearing. I'd rather discuss the matter of Mr. Stojic, not necessarily in the presence of Mr. Prlic. So I'd like to ask the security to lead Mr. Prlic out of the courtroom and to escort Mr. Stojic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salahovic, you'd like to address me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wish to remind you, myself and Mr. Par, we looked into a technical matter yesterday. We are leaving The Hague at 1800 hours this evening, so if you intended to discuss Mr. Prlic, we would like to be present and hear the issues and decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The submissions to the Chamber are there. The Chamber felt it necessary to seek further clarification, clarification mainly given by Mr. Par. I did understand that Mr. Prlic, of course unless he changed his mind, want to be assist by, apart from you, also by Mr. Par, but I could seek confirmation of that. But in the absence of any other message, Mr. Prlic, I take it that you have not changed your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, just a few words, Your Honour. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll take up three minutes today. I took up two minutes yesterday, three today. There is a rule in diplomacy which says you never answer hypothetical questions. Now, if that is true for diplomacy, is it true for law? And your -- I don't think so. And your questions have today helped me understand the situation better. The logic of your question emanates from the constructions upon which the indictments are based. I personally consider that this conflict of interest does not exist because there are no interests, no interests that can in any way be linked up. I have nothing to do, no links with Mr. Martinovic at all. I have no contacts with Mr. Martinovic at all. He was a soldier or whatever you like to call him, a quasi-soldier. I was a civilian myself. So I never could have, nor did I wish to have any relationships with the gentleman in question. Now, as I have been informed, my name was never brought up during that entire case. I would like to thank you for intervening, which above all is to my advantage. You wish to assist me as somebody who stands accused here, and that is why I wish to say that I am taking it possible myself, taking the risk upon myself of this possible hypothetical conflict of interest because I consider that quite simply there is no conflict of interest because there is nothing linking me and Mr. Martinovic. So your positive decision, your positive ruling, has indeed helped me to have the team, the complete Defence team stay intact and that I could avail myself of my right to choose, that I receive probative material so that I can outline the general lines of my defence case. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prlic. Thank you for your words. Because of course it will certainly help the Chamber to assess to what extent your consent is of importance because of the level of understanding of the issue. Could then Mr. Prlic be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're free to leave. I hope you have a good flight home. Yes, you both. If you want to leave, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Stojic. As you are aware of -- we are discussing at this moment -- not discussing, but the Chamber is seeking further clarification on the question on whether you could be represented by Mr. Olujic, Mr. Olujic defending another accused in this Tribunal as well. First of all, just to set the context, Mr. Olujic, would you agree that Mr. Stojic and Mr. Rajic are charged with the same crimes allegedly committed in Stupni Do, in Vares, on and around 23rd of October, 1993, one of them, Mr. Stojic, being presented as the superior of the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You're quite right when you say that with the indictment and the Prosecution thesis expressed therein is moving in that direction. However, I have to say before this august Trial Chamber that I am defending two clients. I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Rajic, and I'm also Defence counsel for Mr. Stojic. Both Mr. Rajic and Mr. Stojic are in the pre-trial stage. Both Mr. Rajic and Mr. Stojic, at their initial appearance, when they appeared before you, Your Honour, declared themselves not guilty on any counts of the indictment. That is to say that they are innocent. However, from your question, I can discern something else, and allow me to explain. I should like to claim that neither subordination nor the other position does not exculpate the subordinated person. That was from Versailles, Nuremberg, to this present Tribunal. That was always the case. But non-discipline, if I can use that word, does not exculpate the superior. So if we were to pose a hypothetical, look at it hypothetically and shift the blame from one to the other, then we wouldn't be able to arrive there because that would mean that both were guilty. So once again, there would be no conflict of interest, and that is something that we are discussing here today. In my opposition -- or, rather, in my response to His Honour -- or, rather, the Prosecutor, that my client Bruno Stojic was a civilian, that is to say that he was a political figure, a top-level political figure. For a short period of time, he was the defence minister of Herceg-Bosna, and on the other side we have Mr. Rajic, and Mr. Rajic was the top military man. That is not challenged. And the Prosecution tried to put forward arguments and say, "No, we have proof and evidence that Stojic was in one -- in a certain way superior to Mr. Rajic." That, first and foremost, is just not correct. But let's take that position as a hypothetical. Let's take it as being that way. And the Prosecutor would have to go to great lengths to prove something like that. But if we were to take a hypothesis like that, I would once again repeat the same thing, that once again there would be no conflict of interests, because Mr. Stojic could not be defended -- have a defence by saying, "I knew about Rajic's crimes," because once again he would be held accountable. And Rajic, as his defence, could not say, "Stojic ordered me to do such-and-such, to commit the crimes," because he would once again be in the same position. He would be responsible and accountable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you a relatively short question, and you engaged in a far wider argument. But if I do understand you where you say there could never be a conflict of interest between the two. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then perhaps put it to you that if Mr. Rajic would, for example, claim in his defence that things he did were done under the orders of a higher level authority, would that be imaginable for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that in the Rajic -- I've been working on the Rajic defence case for one year and that I have studied during that time very voluminous material and archives with the complete documents of the Croatian Defence Council in it, I can simply say that that is impossible because, without a doubt, Rajic functioned exclusively in the chain of command with all its subordination level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- "Military," interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- full detail why you think it's impossible but you Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond consider it impossible for Mr. Rajic for matters for which he's held responsible that the Prosecution would point at higher levels and say, "Well, I did it upon higher instructions."?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would also include -- you know Mr. Rajic is indicted not only on the basis of Article 7(1) but also on the basis of Article 7(3), which means that he is also to be blamed for not investigating once he became aware of matters that happened, and that's part of the charges brought against him. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure whether I understood your question correctly, whether the interpreters interpreted what you have just said to me. So could you be more specific perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Rajic -- part of the indictment against Mr. Rajic is that he did not prevent subordinates from committing crimes and that he did not all necessary measures to investigate and to punish them for those crimes if he was aware of them. I ask your specific attention for this aspect of the charges against Mr. Rajic. Would even considering this part of the indictment -- would be your position that he could never point at higher levels to say, "Well, it's not me, but it's others who instructed me to act this way"?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I took on the defence of Mr. Rajic, I did, of course, explain to him within the code of Defence counsel ethics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, I'm not asking what you explained to Mr. Rajic. You gave an answer to me saying that it could never be part of the defence of Mr. Rajic to point at higher levels and say, "Not I'm responsible but they," and then after having drawn your specific attention to an element of the charges against Mr. Rajic, I asked you whether the answer would, even for those part of the charges, be the same. That's what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Within the frameworks of tactics and strategy, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let me ask you the following: When the Defence in Rajic case claimed that Mr. Rajic conducted investigations but that he was ordered from higher -- one higher official to stop that investigations, do you not consider that to point at higher levels and to say, "I was instructed in this case to stop these investigations," and he's charged with not investigating? Isn't this blaming the higher-up authorities for the conduct of Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rajic -- actually, of course this all went on within the frameworks of his subordination of military organisation to which he belonged, the military establishment. So that it is a question, as you have rightly put it and raised, but at all events, it cannot be a conflict of interest between Mr. Rajic on the one hand and Mr. Stojic on the other. In other words, what you just said, pointing the finger upwards to his superiors, that could only refer to his immediate superior commanding officer, not further up the chain than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be the level of the accused before this Tribunal, that is to say General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not any higher-up authority, military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly not civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I then read to you what you -- what the Defence in the Rajic case wrote down in the motion on the form of the indictment. It reads, and it's about paragraph 22 of the indictment: "This paragraph of the amended indictment conceals the fact that during this time, Mr. Ivica Rajic conducted an investigation against some Croats from the area and that the investigation was subsequently stopped by Mate Boban, President of the Croatian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Let me first ask you, do you consider the president of the Croatian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina a civilian authority or a military authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the way in which power and authority was established, the late Mr. Boban was a civilian person with certain leadership principles. He was a civilian authority at all events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this pointing up at higher-up civilian authorities to blame them for your own conduct or not? I'm just reading your own text.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That was in the context of something else that this was presented. It wasn't in the context -- stated in the context of the appearance or any dual line of command; that is to say that orders came from the civilian authorities in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm drawing your attention to is the following: That in the early stage of the Rajic case you respond to part of the charges by pointing at higher-up civilian authorities in order to explain the conduct of Mr. Rajic. He did conduct an investigation but by higher-up civilian authorities he was stopped to do so. That's what you say. Would you consider there is a conflict of interest to say, "Well, I didn't continue my investigations because I was ordered by higher-up civilian authorities not to do so"?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- I don't think there's a problem there either for the simple reason that both Mr. Stojic and Mr. Rajic were informed in detail about this when they engaged me, and I expressed their will and desire for me -- they expressed the will and desire for me to represent them before this Tribunal. So this hypothetical possibility that the defence of Mr. Rajic would be to the detriment of Mr. Bruno Stojic is not possible. I exclude it as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the consent given by your clients. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because that is my starting position, the desire and wish of my clients. And I determine the tactics and strategy of defence, and their word is law as far as I'm concern. So if I were to put a step -- a foot wrong there and if I was to lose their confidence, then I consider that I would have taken a step into matters that were not allowed, were I to forfeit the interests of either one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the strategy and tactics of Mr. Rajic until now have been to blame higher-up authorities for him not continuing his investigation as we find it in paragraph 22 of the indictment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. However, that was a period of time which could not be relevant to Mr. Stojic, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And why not? Could you please explain that? It was about Stupni Do, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said by way of an introduction, Your Honour, it is absolutely impossible, and that for a number of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like you to first answer my last question. You said it was a period of time which could not be relevant for Mr. Stojic, and then I have drawn your attention to, but please corrected me if I'm wrong, that it was about Stupni Do, and it was a couple of days after that, and that's -- isn't that the time covered by both indictments?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, judging by the facts in the indictment, how they are described. But I consider and claim that that does not mean that a conflict of interest is automatic there between Mr. Stojic and Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It's not automatic there. Okay. Thank you for that answer. Could I ask you the following: In your submissions, you said that the lawyer is here to advise his clients and instruct them on how to minimise all potential conflict of interests. Could you explain whether you -- why and whether you really consider this to be your role as counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My role as Defence counsel is, first and foremost, of course -- and there is no conflict of interest to see to that. That's my first role. And that's what I always look at, and that's what I'm guided by when I take on a client in the first place. I make sure of that. So what I say in response in the motion, let me say that I was brought into a position where I was attacked by the Prosecution, and I had to respond to that attack, and my response was within the frameworks of logics and within the frameworks of the situations that we see in life, and all parties -- or both parties in the proceedings, both the accused and his Defence counsel on the one side and on the other the Prosecution. That's what the reality of the situation was. So in that response, I used the -- this formulation, and I stand by it fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you mean by "coordinating two defences in order to make the punishment less severe?" Let's say the Defence is uncoordinated and one client could be in a fairly better position than the other? What do you consider then your role to be? Let me just give you an example. Let's just say Mr. Rajic, for not continuing his investigation by stressing that point very much and that he was instructed to do so, can get a lower sentence - well, let's say on the assumption that he would have -- that he would be convicted, whereas the higher-up authorities might incur a more heavier sentence. What would be your role to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my role is always such that I defend to the maximum the interests of in this case of both my clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. -- Mr. Rajic is very much helped, that's just meant for argument's sake, is very much helped by blaming everyone on the top level. On the other hand, Mr. Stojic might be very much helped by -- well, let's say denying that he gave such instructions or that I left -- that he left it to the discretion of the subordinate, whatever. But what would you do? First of all, for Mr. Rajic. Would you nevertheless insist on the higher-level responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this specific case we cannot view this hypothetically. Rajic has pleaded not guilty on all counts of the indictment, and he will prove this before this Tribunal. Likewise, Mr. Stojic will do the same. Therefore, this possibility does not exist for the simple reason that they are both innocent, that they both deny the charges and are preparing to prove before this Tribunal that they are innocent. They hope they will be successful in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why do you do -- write down then, and that investigation, the investigation conducted by Mr. Rajic, was subsequently stopped by the president of the Croatian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? That's what you write down. It's not invented by me. It's not hypothetical. It's part of your submissions in the Rajic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it is what he wants, and I am duty-bound to follow the instructions given to me by my client. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's just assume that Mr. Stojic would want you to contradict that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can put that forward as a hypothesis, but it's not possible because Mr. Stojic cannot do so in view of the defence we have been constructing for a full five months now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you for those answers. When you say having one counsel is the best way of ensuring that the two clients are not asked to be witnesses against each other, what's the -- what do I have to understand by that if it would turn out to be favourable for one of your clients that the other would testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By this I mean, first of all, what the opposing side wants in every trial, and that is to prove their case by entering into an agreement, adding a number of arguments that the Prosecution wishes to put forward in the judgement of the Court. That's what I meant. And with the knowledge gained in both cases, I will be able to help both clients to select what is best for them and what will give them the best possible position in the trial that lies ahead of them. That's what prompted me to write this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that by the best way of ensuring that the two clients are not asked to be witnesses against each other, that is that you consider being counsel of two accused the best way of preventing them from entering into any agreement that would lead to testimony to be given by your clients.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The aim of both my clients is the truth, not trade. Establishing the truth, not finding a way of strewing themselves with ashes and being punished but to prove the truth. We will prove that both indictments do not hold water, and we will do so only with the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. You also use the argument that one Judge in two cases would be a relevant issue. At least a relevant element to consider. Could you explain to me why you think that could have an impact on the existence or non-existence of a conflict of interest?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I of course respect all the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal, but as it so happens, both my cases are before Trial Chamber I. When I wrote this, I felt that the Court would be able to observe my professional work, and this also in view of any possible conflict of interest, which is, of course, the duty of the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber must watch over the way the case is conducted, and should anything arise and should my professional dignity ever be put into question, which I'm sure is not possible in view of my 30 years of experience, but to err is human. The Court, however, does not err, and the Court would then be able to observe that I was doing something to the detriment of one or the other of my clients because the same Trial Chamber would be dealing with both cases. This is why I mentioned this in my brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That might be too high a level of expectation to think that a Trial Chamber could have a thorough knowledge of every aspect and of every element of the confidential relationship between client and counsel, but let me move to my next question to you. You said you obtained the consent of your client, and you called that an "unconditional consent." What does this actually mean? What is an unconditional consent? Would that be mean that, for example, if later on they -- a possibility of at least some conflict of interest could become clear they should say, "No, you -- you consented now and we'll continue"? Or how do we have to understand the unconditional consent?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way I interpret it is that I consider it the will of my client at that point in time. When he said that, that was for me the law. However, should a client change his mind, I would withdraw from the case voluntarily. I am bound to do so by my code of honour and by the code of both the bars I belong to, the one of this Tribunal as well. So it is the client who decides the manner in which I will defend him and the extent to which I will defend him. It is the client's will that is decisive, and the client, of course, may always change his mind. This, however, is not connected to one Defence counsel having two cases. It refers to any Defence counsel in any case. Many counsel have had the experience of withdrawing from a case because the client changed his mind. It is the client's will that is of paramount importance. Should either Stojic or Rajic say to me tomorrow, "I don't want you to defend me any more," I would respect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although the Chamber could instruct you to continue the defence in order to prevent the disruption of the trial. But my question was whether you could explain what "unconditional" means in this context. I do understand now that you say if they give their consent but if they withdraw that -- well, if they tomorrow say that they do not want to be represented by you any more you would follow that instruction, but what is now the unconditional consent? What's the difference between a consent and an unconditional consent? What conditions could we have had in mind saying that this is an unconditional one?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their wish and will at that point in time was to engage me as their Defence counsel. I think there is no difference. It is certainly not something that is absolute. Of course, in real life the situation Your Honour has mentioned could arise; that is, that the Chamber requests that I continue a defence. Then I would be bound by the decision of the Trial Chamber, which I would be duty-bound to respect. It would be binding on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's say at a later stage there would be a matter which keeps your two clients apart but they both would agree to be -- to be represented by you, to continue your representation of both. Let's just take the example again, which is not a hypothetical example but an example I read in your submissions. Mr. Rajic says, "Well, I will stop the investigating, so don't blame me for not further investigating and punishing people because I was ordered to do so." Whether or not that would totally excuse him is a different matter, but at least it explained why -- it could explain why he didn't follow what he started to do. And then, if the -- at the higher level including circles Mr. Stojic is charged to be in a joint criminal enterprise with, if there was no -- no it's -- of course it's not our interest then to -- we are blamed for stopping Rajic rather than the other way, is that how -- but both clients would then say, "Well, let's continue." What would you do? So a conflict of interest has become apparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not their interest if they feel that the situation is such that their best strategy and line of defence is the one they have chosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So Mr. Rajic chooses to blame the higher up, and Mr. Stojic would choose not to take responsibility for that, for ever giving or joint criminal enterprise giving any instructions to stop investigations. You'd continue the two lines of defence, contradicting each other considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If their cases were contradictory or if there was any sort of conflict between them, I would not continue. I would continue, however, if I could do so by helping both clients. I am watching out for the interests of both clients equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another question: In the Rajic case, reference is made -- no, let me stay out -- would you withdraw from both clients or from -- would you choose from one of them under the circumstances you just described?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it were not contrary to my own moral principles, the work I have done and the success I have achieved in the defence, then I would defend the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- no. My question was: If a conflict of interest has arisen, I asked you what you would do, whether you would continue, yes or no. You said, "No, I would not continue." But from which case would you withdraw in the -- well, would you withdraw from Mr. Rajic? Would you withdraw from Mr. Stojic? Or would you say, "First in, last out"? Or what would be your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both my clients are equally important to me. To me, it is immaterial which one came -- was first in. I am equally responsible to both of them for everything I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's no answer to my question. My question is on the basis of what would you choose either to withdraw? Would you withdraw from both cases? Would you withdraw from one case? And if you would withdraw from one case, on the basis of what criteria?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is too hypothetical for me to answer, Your Honour. I would have to find myself in such a situation first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are thinking about risks of conflict of interests, then you're always talking about a situation that does not yet exist but nevertheless have to be calculated before taking any decisions. Mr. Stojic, you have heard the whole of my questions. Are you fully informed about all the submissions made by your counsel in respect of this conflict of interest? Have you seen all his arguments presented? Has he discussed them with you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have seen everything that Mr. Olujic told you. I have to tell you I am an economist by profession, not a lawyer. It is only for the past four or five months that I have worked with Mr. Olujic, so I cannot at this point give you a proper reply. I'm sure, however, that there is no conflict of interest between Rajic and me. I was not his superior. The Main Staff was his superior. And I had nothing to do with the Main Staff. It was responsible to the Supreme Command, directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment. As I read out to you, whether it's true or not is a different matter. Mr. Rajic -- part of the defence of Mr. Rajic is that when he was allegedly under a duty to investigate certain crimes that he was stopped by Mate Boban at that time, at least according to your counsel, the president of the -- the president of the Croatian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The indictment states that you, together with others, among who Mr. Boban were engaged in a joint criminal enterprise. That means that if there would be a shared intent and if certain conditions would be fulfilled, that you're held to some extent responsible for also what the others in the joint criminal enterprise did. Now, Mr. Rajic is pointing at one of the members of the joint criminal enterprise and saying, "He stopped me from doing what I, according to the indictment, should have done." That makes him pointing at, well, a group of persons, in the view of the Prosecution, including you, who is blamed by Mr. Rajic for instructing him to do certain matters. So if you say it's all hypothetical, it's not hypothetical at this moment. It's -- I would say what -- I point it as a risk by further verification seems not only to be a risk but seems to materialise already. So I want you to be aware of that. But of course you're free to express your point of view, but if you say it's all just hypothetical, it's -- but please continue. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when Stupni Do happened, at that point in time, a few days later, I left the position of minister of defence. I did not take part in the subsequent events. I'm sure if Rajic said that, he wasn't referring to me. I haven't read what he submitted, but I'm sure he couldn't have meant me. He couldn't have meant me, because I was just about to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The period of the indictment, however, still continues. May I take it that you're still -- you have not changed your mind? You still want to be represented by Mr. Olujic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I say something? I chose Zeljko Olujic of my own free will because I know him before. I know his moral character. I know his professional abilities. Many friends of mine have told me about him, what sort of person he is and what kind of lawyer he is. This was my will and my choice. I have been working with Mr. Olujic for four or five months, and we have come a long way towards preparing my defence. I wish to point out that I want to defend myself only with the truth. I don't want anyone to construct a defence for me other than that. I'm sure that no one can impose on me any kind of defence I do not want. Mr. Olujic is an honourable man. When I read the indictment, I was shocked, and so was my family. At that point, what mattered most to me was the welfare of my family. Ten days ago, my family came to visit me, and they talked more about Zeljko Olujic than they did about me. I came to understand that he was helping them live a normal life, and if at all possible, I wish to continue working with Mr. Olujic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will deliberate on whether that would be possible as you requested. Mr. Olujic, I have no further questions to you, nor do I have any further questions for Mr. Stojic. Then Mr. Jonjic, you're the last one, and I think as a matter of fact that we would not need much time, as a matter of fact. But I would like to ask the security to escort Mr. Stojic out of the courtroom and to ask Mr. -- ask them to escort Mr. Coric into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Coric. Please be seated. We are discussing at this moment the possible conflicts of interest by counsel that are representing more than one accused before this Tribunal. I -- since you have not made any request, Mr. -- I do understand there are some problems with the earphones. Can you now hear me, Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just explained that we are discussing at this moment the possible conflicts of interest of counsel representing more than one accused before this Tribunal, which is of some concern to the Chamber. Mr. Jonjic, we have carefully read also the observations by the Registry, the Registry which is less concerned about the conflict of interest in the case of Mr. Coric and Mr. Ljubicic. The -- do I well understand that the main point of where same events are covered by both indictments is the Ahmici 1993 issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the indictment, the amended indictment against Mr. Pasko Ljubicic includes some other events which occurred in the first half of 1993 in the area of the Busovaca and Vitez municipality in Central Bosnia, in the Lasva River Valley. But, of course, Ahmici is the most important event, and it's the greatest crime that happened in that area. There is no doubt about the fact that that is the central point or the mainstay of the indictment against Mr. Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I put a question to you? When I yesterday heard you expressing your confidence in the cooperation of the Croatian government, it came into my mind that in the Ljubicic case you were far less convinced, it seemed, of the cooperation of the Croatian government. I remember that it took approximately one year to figure out they are not cooperative in whatever way. Is there any problem, as far as you're concerned, on the one hand in the one case having to defend that the Croatian government is the most reliable government and which gives all assistance including documents, as was specifically mentioned yesterday, whereas I know that in the Ljubicic case, especially getting documents was quite a problem. Could I have your comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. Yesterday when I was expressing confidence in the readiness of the Croatian government to extend the guarantees that it has extended in this case, then that confidence was limited exclusively to the validity of those guarantees. Perhaps you know that as far as those guarantees or similar guarantees in the case of -- in the Ljubicic case we had serious problems with the Croatian government. At first the Croatian government extended these guarantees after which it then withdrew them. In the meantime, of course, there was some political changes in the Republic of Croatia so that I think that after those changes I can, without any reserves, believe in the readiness of the Croatian government to respect the guarantees it has extended to the six accused in this case. This, of course, does not mean that I have no reservations regarding the readiness of some parts of the Croatian state administration. It wouldn't be quite precise to say that we are talking about the failings of the present government because the problems that Mr. Ljubicic and I as his Defence counsel had with the Republic of Croatia date back to the behaviour of the previous government, the government which at last year's elections was defeated, last elections of November. The engagement of that government or parts of that earlier government regarding archived documents amounted to what, according to my and Mr. Ljubicic's deep conviction, was not something that was in accordance with the Croatian laws and the constitution and the laws covering the republic's cooperation with this Tribunal. After the present government came to power, the conditions have normalised and now we have unlimited access to all the materials which were earlier located in the ministry of defence and which were given to the Croatian State Archive on December -- in December 2003. We don't know whether a part of the documentation was physically destroyed or not during the rule of the previous government. This is something that is still to be established. However, my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jonjic, I'm going to stop you. You'll understand not the details of these matters are that relevant at the moment but the dilemma it could create. May I ask you, did you discuss with your client the possibility that the two cases you're involved in, that is the Ljubicic case and the case against Mr. Coric, for example, could be heard at the same time? And would you consider it possible for yourself to do two trials at the same time? Many counsel have already difficulties in managing one at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did discuss this with Mr. Ljubicic and Mr. Coric, that is the possibility that both cases would be tried at the same time. And of course we discussed the possibility or the risk of a theoretical conflict of interest appearing. We discussed this at the theoretical level. I don't believe that this is a real danger in view of the fact that the Ljubicic case is in its final stages. The pre-trial motions have been submitted a year ago, and we believe that the trial should start quite soon. However, it is quite clear to me that if this theoretical situation should really come to be, for these two cases to be tried at the same time, it would not be serious to say that both of the cases could be conducted with the same quality if they were -- if these two trials were held at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would you do?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In such a case, of course, we are speaking from the position that this will not happen. I said to Mr. Coric quite openly, without any hesitation, that with all my regret, I would have to stay loyal to Mr. Ljubicic regardless of the difficulties that that would pose for me and Mr. Coric, because Mr. Ljubicic's case began first. The pre-trial phase has been under way for 33 months now, and it would be quite unfair for me to abandon him and to hand over my role as Defence counsel to someone else. Of course, Mr. Ljubicic is aware of this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Coric, may I ask you the following question: Could you explain to me exactly to what extent and where the links are between the case against Mr. Ljubicic and your own case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am aware of both indictments, of my own and the one for Mr. Ljubicic. The events that overlap in both indictments are very small, minor. I am aware of a possible conflict of interest. A theoretical risk of that does exist in these two cases, but I am convinced that the further developments of this case here and, based on my overview of the two cases, I believe that there will be no conflict. I would like to ask you to believe in my personal choice of my Defence counsel. I believe in his professional qualifications, and I believe that this will not be prejudicial to either myself or to Mr. Ljubicic, if he represents both of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say a theoretical risk does exist. Where would that risk be?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not dare to go into specific events from the period for which both of us are indicted, but I know that this overlap is minor, practically negligible. I know that Mr. Ljubicic's indictment is based on events that took place in Central Bosnia, and as far as I could see in my indictment, this area is not part of the indictment against me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you explained where there would be no conflict of interest possible instead of explaining to me where you saw that risk, but I'd rather leave it to it for the time being. Let me just -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got no further questions for you. The -- you've answered the questions, the -- you've certainly assisted the Chamber in clarifying the issue so that we can make our decisions. Just for completeness' sake, is there anything else you would like to raise at this moment? I didn't ask other counsel, so I would like to ask you, Mr. Jonjic, to keep it to a minimum. Mr. Scott, I take it that taking into account your specific position here, that there is no need to further address me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes this hearing. The Chamber will give a decision on the issue to the extent necessary. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 3.56 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Defence counsel for the accused Prlic withdrew]
